Asymmetric C atalysis
Organocatalytic Enantioselective 1,12-Addition of Alkynyl Biphenyl
Quinone Methides Formed In Situ
Xing Wang
+
, Boming Shen
+
, Meiwen Liu
+
, Ziyang Wang, Chang Liu, Pengfei Li,*
Peiyuan Yu,* and Wenjun Li*
Abstract: The chemistry of quinone methides formed in
situ has been flourishing in recent years. In sharp
contrast, the development and utilization of biphenyl
quinone methides are rare. In this study, we achieved a
remote stereocontrolled 1,12-conjugate addition of bi-
phenyl quinone methides formed in situ for the first
time. In the presence of a suitable chiral phosphoric
acid, alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides were generated
from α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols,
followed by enantioselective 1,12-conjugate addition
with indole-2-carboxylates. The strategy enabled the
alcohols to serve as efficient allenylation reagents,
providing practical access to a broad range of axially
chiral allenes bearing a (1,1’-biphenyl)-4-ol unit, which
were previously less accessible. Combined with control
experiments, density functional theory calculations shed
light on the reaction mechanism, indicating that enantio-
selectivity originates from the nucleophilic addition of
alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides. Notably, not only
the presence of biphenyl quinone methides as versatile
intermediates was confirmed but also organocatalytic
enantioselective 1,12-addition was established.
O ver the past decade, quinone methides (QMs) have been
identified as practical and high-value-added intermediates
for the synthesis of functionalized molecules.
[1]
Notably, with
the aid of chiral phosphoric acids (CPAs),
[2]
stereoselective
reactions including nucleophilic addition, annulation and
one-pot cascade reaction of QMs generated in situ from the
corresponding hydroxybenzyl alcohols have been well-
established for diversified and directed asymmetric synthesis
(Scheme 1A).
[3]
In particular, the conjugate addition of these
QMs, catalyzed by CPAs, offers a robust method for
accessing axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes.
[4]
However,
organocatalytic stereoselective reactions of their extended
analogues with carbonyl and methide units incorporated in
different aromatic rings remain rare. Recently, Sun et al.
have elegantly disclosed a CPA-catalyzed 1,6-conjugate
addition of 2-naphthoquinone-8-methides (2-Nap-Q-8-Ms)
formed in situ from 8-(hydroxyarylmethyl)naphthalen-2-ols
(Scheme 1B).
[5]
At the same time, we independently devel-
oped a CPA-catalyzed 1,8-conjugate addition of 2-naphtho-
quinone-6-methides (2-Nap-Q-6-Ms) formed in situ from 6-
(hydroxydiarylmethyl)naphthalen-2-ols for the synthesis of
chiral tetraarylmethanes.
[6]
More importantly, the utilization
of these versatile naphthoquinone methides (Nap-QMs) has
provided a novel platform for the construction of enantioen-
riched complex target molecules.
As another type of extended QMs, biaryl quinone
methides (BQMs) have been photogenerated from the
corresponding 4-(4’-hydroxyphenyl)benzyl alcohols,
[7]
which
cannot be readily generated via thermal chemistry. In
particular, the application of BQMs as intermediates in the
asymmetric synthesis has remained unknown (Scheme 1C).
Obviously, the catalytic asymmetric transformation of such
BQMs presents several challenges. Firstly, it is crucial to
efficiently generate these BQMs in situ from the corre-
sponding alcohols under mild conditions. Secondly, achiev-
ing selectivity in terms of chemo- and regioselectivity is a
pivotal concern in the reactions of BQMs.
[8]
Thirdly, a
formidable challenge arises in terms of stereocontrol for the
remote addition of more extensively conjugated systems. In
fact, organocatalytic remote stereocontrolled conjugate
addition are still in its infancy.
[9]
Particularly, only three
reports on organocatalyzed enantioselective 1,10-addition
have been disclosed.
[10]
To our best knowledge, the organo-
catalytic enantioselective 1,12-addition has not been devel-
oped so far. To fill this gap, the development of an
organocatalytic stereoselective 1,12-addition of BQMs
formed in situ from α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl
alcohols is urgent and in great demand.
Based on our previous work on organocatalytic stereo-
selective reactions of propargyl alcohols,
[8d,10b,11]
we first
calculated the energy barrier for the dehydration assisted by
dimethyl phosphate using density functional theory (DFT).
As shown in Scheme 1D, the energy barrier for dehydration
of 4’-(1-hydroxy-1,3-diphenylprop-2-yn-1-yl)-[1,1’-biphenyl]-
4-ol to form alkynyl 4,4’-BQMs is 30.1 kcal/mol, indicating
that the in situ formation of alkynyl 4,4’-BQM under mild

are � 7.0 and � 6.5 ppm. These results show that an apparent
decrease in aromaticity of biphenyl rings from propargyl
alcohol to alkynyl 4,4’-BQM, and rearomatization of alkynyl
4,4’-BQM would provide strong driving force for the
subsequent reaction. In addition, the use of an appropriate
catalytic system, reaction partners, and optimal conditions is
crucial for achieving successful stereocontrol. Accordingly,
we herein reported a chiral phosphoric acid catalyzed
reaction of α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols
via asymmetric 1,12-addition of in situ formed alkynyl 4,4’-
BQMs (Scheme 1E). Notably, this work validated the ability
of alkynyl 4,4’-BQMs to act as versatile intermediates in
organocatalytic asymmetric reactions featuring remote ster-
eocontrolled 1,12-conjugate addition for the synthesis of
axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes.
[4a,13]
At the beginning of the investigation, we focused on
CPAs as a result of their demonstrated excellent perform-
ance in the conjugate addition of electron-deficient systems
formed in situ from the corresponding functionalized
alcohols.
[3–6,8,10–11,14–17]
As shown in Table 1, the CPA-1
catalyzed reaction between the model substrates 1-[4-(4-
hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]-1,3-diphenylprop-2-yn-1-ol 1 a and
cyclohexyl 1H-indole-2-carboxylate 2 a furnished allene 3 aa
in 54 % yield (Table 1, entry 1). Although racemic product
was obtained, it confirmed the effectivity of phosphoric acid.
To improve the enantioselectivity, a series of chiral
phosphoric acids were investigated (Table 1, entries 2–5).
Specifically, the desired product (S)-3 aa was obtained in
70 % yield with 40 % ee in the presence of catalyst CPA-3
(Table 1, entry 3). Furthermore, catalyst CPA-5 enabled the
formation of the target product (S)-3 aa in 83 % yield with
42 % ee (Table 1, entry 5). To our delight, enantioselectivity

with 73 % ee (Table 1, entry 6, see Supporting Information
for more details). Further modification of reaction condi-
tions enabled the formation of (S)-3 aa in 82 % yield with
82 % ee (Table 1, entry 7, see Supporting Information for
more details). To further improve the efficiency and stereo-
selectivity, we re-examined the catalytic system (Table 1,
entries 8–10), disclosing that the desired product (S)-3 aa
was obtained in 71 % yield with 63 % yield from the CPA-8
catalyzed reaction (Table 1, entry 10). Systematic screening
studies including the effect of solvents, concentration,
reaction temperature and various added additives revealed
that CPA-8 enabled the formation of (S)-3 aa in 88 % yield
with 84 % ee at 25 ° C in toluene after 96 h (Table 1, entry 11,
see Supporting Information for more details). When spiro
catalyst CPA-9 was employed, the racemic product was
obtained in 51 % yield (Table 1, entry 12). Similar results
were obtained with spiro catalyst CPA-10 (Table 1, en-
try 13).
With the established conditions, we surveyed the sub-
strate scope of the reactions between propargyl alcohols and
indole-2-carboxylates. In the presence of CPA-5, the effect
of the ester group of indole-2-carboxylates was first inves-
tigated (Scheme 2A). Concretely, the ester group (R
3
) was
found to have a slight effect on the reaction, affording the
corresponding products (S)-3 aa–ae in 76–90 % yields with
70–86 % ee. Alternatively, the desired (S)-3 aa–ae could be
obtained in 78–88 % yields with 64–86 % ee with the aid of
catalyst CPA-8. Furthermore, various substituents (R
4
= F,
Cl, Br, Me, MeO) could be introduced to the indole ring of
indole-2-carboxylates and the desired (S)-3 af–aj were
obtained in 71–87 % yields with 72–90 % ee. Neither
significant electronic nor steric effect of the aromatic moiety
was observed. In all, a wide range of indole-2-carboxylates
reacted smoothly to generate the corresponding axially
chiral allenes 3 in high yields and enantioselectivities. To
explore the synthetic potential, the CPA-5 catalyzed reac-
tion was scaled up to 1.25 mmol that furnished the corre-
sponding product (S)-3 ad with equally high efficiency and
stereoselectivity as the small-scale reaction (80 % yield, 85 %
ee).
With these encouraging data in hand, we turned our
attention to the scope of α-[4-(4-

Notably, under standard conditions, the asymmetric 1,8-
conjugate addition of indole-2-carboxylate 2 d to alkynyl
quinone methides formed in situ from 4-(1-hydroxy-1,3-
diphenylprop-2-yn-1-yl)phenol 1 a’ furnished the desired
allene 3 a’d in 74 % yield with 81 % ee, which indicated that
the chiral phosphoric acid-catalyzed conjugate addition was
successfully expanded from 1,8-addition to 1,12-addition
with the aid of (1,1’-biphenyl)-4-ol unit. Taken altogether,
these results not only verified that the (1,1’-biphenyl)-4-ol
unit served as a practical functional group to enable the
formation of axially chiral allenes from propargyl alcohols,
but also indicated that organocatalytic remote stereocontrol
was achieved via the CPA-5 catalyzed 1,12-conjugate
addition of alkynyl 4,4’-BQMs formed in situ.
Esterification of free hydroxyl groups of axially chiral
allenes (S)-3 ad was investigated with several classical
reagents (Scheme 4A). Notably, the corresponding products
(S)-4 ad, (S)-5 ad and (S)-6 ad were obtained in high
efficiency without compromising the enantioselectivity. To
further examine the effect of (1,1’-biphenyl)-4-ol unit,
control experiments were surveyed (Scheme 4B). When α-
[4-(4-phenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohol 1 m was employed to
react with indole-2-carboxylate 2 d under the standard
conditions, allene (S)-3 md was obtained in 42 % yield with
33 % ee. The reason might be that the absence of alkynyl
biphenyl quinone methide formation likely contributed to
the reaction proceeding via the S

The absolute configuration of product 3 aa was assigned
by comparison between its experimental and calculated
electronic circular dichroism (ECD) spectra to be the S
configuration (Figure 1). Furthermore, kinetic studies indi-
cated that this reaction is first order in propargylic alcohol
1 a (Figure 2A), first order in chiral catalyst CPA-5 (Fig-
ure 2B), and order of about 0.7 in nucleophile 2 f (Fig-
ure 2C).
To better understand the mechanism and origins of
stereoselectivity, DFT calculations were carried out upon
CPA-5 mediated reaction between alcohol 1 a and indole-2-
carboxylate 2 d (see Supporting Information for details). As

shown in Figure 3, the reaction was initiated by the
formation of hydrogen bond complex int-1 from substrate
1 a and chiral phosphoric acid CPA-5 with an endergonic
process of 3.9 kcal/mol. The intermediate int-1 then under-
goes dehydration via transition state TS1 to afford an
identical intermediate alkynyl BQM int-2 with an energy
barrier of 18.8 kcal/mol. With the participation of indole-2-
carboxylate nucleophile 2 d, the catalyst could protonate
BQM and form a hydrogen-bonded complex int-3S. Sub-
sequently, the intermolecular nucleophilic addition via
transition state TS2-S with a corresponding energy barrier of
13.8 kcal/mol generates the intermediate int-4S. Finally,
intermediate int-4S could undergo rearomatization/proton
transfer via transition state TS3-S with an energy barrier of
5.3 kcal/mol, generating the product (S)-3 ad and regenerat-
ing the catalyst CPA-5. The computational results disclosed
the intermolecular nucleophilic addition of indole-2-carbox-
ylate 2 d to alkynyl BQM int-2 is considered to be the
enantio- and rate-determining step for this reaction. It is
noteworthy that this step requires a smaller activation
energy than the preceding dehydration step in terms of
energy of single steps. However, due to the high-energy
intermediate int-3, the transition state TS-2 for this step
becomes the highest-energy point on the computed free-
energy profile. The rate-determining step involves the
reversibly generated high-energy BQM intermediate, the
catalyst, and the indole-2-carboxylate, which is consistent
with results from the kinetic studies. Regarding the stereo-
chemistry, the intermolecular nucleophilic addition via
transition state TS2-R with an energy barrier of 15.3 kcal/
mol would generate intermediate int-4R, which is the
precursor of the product (R)-3 ad. The relative free energy
of the transition state TS2-R is 2.0 kcal/mol higher than that
of transition state TS2-S, which indicates that the generation
of the R-configured product is unfavorable. The calculated
enantiomeric excess (ee) is 93 % based on the energy
difference between transition states TS2-R and TS2-S, which
slightly overestimated the experimental result (86 % ee).
Furthermore, optimized structures of transition states TS2-S
and TS2-R were compared (Figure 4A). Notably, the
N � H···O � S and C � H···O � P hydrogen-bonding interactions
existed in stereoisomeric transition states TS2-R and TS2-S.
Particularly, transition state TS2-S enjoys additional stabiliz-
ing C � H···O � P hydrogen-bonding interactions with contact
distances of 2.21 and 2.30 Å, respectively. These more stable
hydrogen-bonding interactions contributed significantly to
the stabilization of transition state TS2-S, which is likely the
most important factor that determining the stereoselectivity.
In contrast, there is a lack of additional stabilizing
C � H···O � P hydrogen-bonding interactions in the disfavored
transition state TS2-R. Further calculations by removing the
substituents of the catalyst with methyl groups, then
computing the single-point energy difference ΔΔE

state TS2-S is still 2.1 kcal/mol lower in energy than
transition state TS2-R, indicating that hydrogen-bonding
interactions play a leading role in achieving high enantiose-

ity, we performed the quantitative Bader’s atoms-in-mole-
cules (AIM)
[18]
analyses for the transition states TS2-S and
TS2-R. The value of Laplacian of electron densities (r

TS2-R, and the corresponding pathway associated with TS2-
S has a lower energy barrier. To further verify the accuracy
of our computational results, single-point energies were also

catalytic reactions involving their extended analogues,
biphenyl quinone methides, remains unexplored. Herein, we
have established such a reaction for the first time. In detail,
alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides were generated in situ
from α-[4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)phenyl]propargyl alcohols with
the aid of a chiral phosphoric acid catalyst, followed by
enantioselective 1,12-conjugate addition of indole-2-carbox-
ylates to furnish a wide range of axially chiral tetrasubsti-
tuted allenes with high efficiency. Control experiments and
DFT calculations were utilized to investigate the reaction
pathway. Through hydrogen-bonding interactions, a new
organocatalytic remote stereocontrol model was developed.
Of note, not only alkynyl biphenyl quinone methides formed
in situ were developed as versatile intermediates for
asymmetric synthesis, but also organocatalytic enantioselec-
tive 1,12-additions were achieved for the construction of
axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes. Additional studies on
biphenyl quinone methides are underway in our laborato-
ries.
